newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Age-old English fair celebrates marrows and sheep.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Age-old English fair celebrates marrows and sheep.

text.p: Each year on the second Tuesday in September, this sleepy village nestled in one of England's most spectacular national parks celebrates the fruits of nature with a festival.
The Widecombe Fair is not a big event but its simple charms are as unchanging as the white cliffs of Dover and as timeless as the rolling green hills of Shakespeare's sceptered isle.

The fair is held next to the school house on a two-acre (0.894 hectares) cow pasture that borders this tiny hamlet in Dartmoor National Park, only 200 miles (320 km) -- but around two centuries -- southwest of London.

Size, at least to the fair's vegetable judges, only counts when looking at marrow. "Colour and shape are taken into consideration but the weight of the marrow is the key," says Wilf, one of the Fair's organisers.
Wilf had a busy morning deciding who would win blue ribbons for the biggest marrow, most appealing potatoes, tidy turnips, and a dozen or so other prize vegetables.
Carrots on the catwalk have been a feature of the Widecombe Fair since the early 19th century and a part of the charm that attracted more than 10,000 people to this year's festivities.
Unlike many carnivals across Britain and Europe at this time of year, Widecombe shies away from electronic attractions. There are no carousels, roller coasters or virtual-reality simulators.
Widecombe looks back rather than forward. There is not a single satellite dish on any of the village's stone cottages and none of its few hundred residents have Internet addresses.
But the world comes to Widecombe because of its age-old charm, traversing Dartmoor on single-track roads and avoiding sheep which roam free over the windswept moor.

"Sheep are really the main attraction of the Fair," said Peter, another organiser, pointing to a pen of White-Faced Dartmoors. "To me, these are attractive because, personally, I like a long, bigger sheep."
Each sheep produces about five kilos (11 lb) of fleece, which is used primarily for making carpets, he said.

Competition from synthetic materials has pushed the price of the wool down to around 1.00 pound ($1.56) a kilo. Until the 1930s the fleece of Widecombe sheep was highly valued by Italian fathers-of-the-bride.
"In Italy it used to be the duty of a bride's father to provide a mattress for the bridal couple," Peter said. "The ultimate in luxury was a Devon, long-wool mattress."
While the price of wool "wasn't what it used to be", the value of lamb has rocketed as consumers switch from beef because of Britain's "mad-cow" beef scare.

Peter said live lamb, which would normally sell for around 80 pence ($1.25) a kilo (2.2lb) was now fetching 1.20 pounds ($1.95) after the British government warned last March that cattle infected with bovine spongiform encepholapthy (BSE) could cause a fatal form of brain disease in humans.
However, most of Widecombe's sheep farmers also raise beef cattle, the price of which has plunged by up to 30 percent, he said. "People here are angry and they blame the government," said Peter.

British beef, in the form of sandwiches or hamburgers was the only thing on the menu at the food tent, which was doing a brisk trade. The food queue stretched well past the sheep shearing and blacksmith displays right up to the Fair's only gambling establishment, the Widecombe School "Cow Pat Casino'.
"You can win 50 pounds ($78.00) for just a one pound wager," said croupier Sheila Crowley. "All you have to do is predict where on the parade ground the cow will "perform'."

The parade ground, separated from the rest of the fair by a single strand of rope, was also used for the fancy dress procession (mounted and unmounted) and for the display of vintage machinery and shire horses.
Fresh-faced local girls in colourful costumes performed the Maypole dance shortly before the local lads showed off their muscles in the annual bale of hay tossing contest.
The Widecombe orgainisers published a strict timetable of events but the times inevitably slipped on a warm autumnal day where the sun was occasionally obscured by a passing cloud.
"Would someone please go to the beer tent and find Bill -- the terrier race is about to start," boomed a slightly disgruntled voice over the Fair's public address system.

The Ballad of Widecombe Fair, a famous British folk song written around 150 years ago, tells the tale of eight men, good and true, who celebrated their arrival there "liberally" until none could stand to make the homeward march.
Bill never made the 100 yard (metre) trek from the beer tent to the parade ground. Like Widecombe Fair, some things never change.
